result.killer: Partial: free MHT 'Payment of Fee/Taxes' e-service, plus the external auditor's required certification of the statements, plus certified PMS for the Mueen guest-data feed. No single named product does the whole compliance pack.
result.reason: I found no product that kills it outright. Searches in Arabic and English found no Oman-specific tool that builds the 4% quarterly statement or the 8% distribution statement. Hotelogix's Oman PMS page doesn't mention the 4% fee, MHT reporting or Mueen. Still, the gap is thin. The free MHT e-service already takes the fee payment. External auditors must certify the statements, so they act as gatekeepers and are the natural done-for-you option. Daily guest data goes to Mueen through MHT-certified PMS (vendors not named). The 4% and 8% sums are trivial in any PMS or spreadsheet. The market is small: roughly 800-1,500 establishments nationwide, most of them tiny guest houses and green inns. Unsettled: whether small inns face the auditor and declaration rules, and how many classified restaurants there are.

candidates.buyer: Owner-operators and small firms running water or sewage tankers, who need a permit from the regional water utility
candidates.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers (also 13 and 18)

Licensees (the utility operating companies) must run the electronic register and install the tracking devices, so the likely software sits with the utilities and not the operators. A Saudi 'Tasreeh' platform from National Water Company is a different country.
candidates.name: Independent water and sewage tanker operator permit and SLA compliance kit
candidates.trigger: APSR Decision 31/2025 (Gazette 1593, 27 Apr 2025, effective the next day). No tanker may operate without a permit and a signed unified SLA (Art. 2-3). Existing operators had one year, to about late Apr 2026, to comply. Colour-coding and Arabic labelling (Art. 6). Tank cleaning and disinfection, inspection and complaint records (Art. 5(5), 7). Data supplied on request (Art. 7(5)). Fines OMR 50-5,000 for individuals and OMR 500-50,000 for companies, doubled on repeat, up to OMR 50 a day (Art. 8). Muscat Municipality sewage-vehicle rules of 29 Jun 2026 add a licence plate and approved disposal points.
candidates.unchecked: Operator count and whether permits are renewed each year (the text says nothing on validity); whether operators must file periodic reports or only respond on request; whether utilities already have a portal and tracker vendors for this; the exact start of the one-year deadline; whether fines are being enforced now that the deadline has passed.

coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: New domestic-worker decision (reported as MD 475/2025 or 574/2025, number conflicting; in force from about 9-13 Oct 2025): Arabic contracts registered electronically on MoL platform, no recruitment fees charged to workers, 12h/day cap, 21 days leave, records kept 1 year after service, 3-month transition, under-21 ban. Nothing new beyond K04 for households.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: 2022 activity-licence regulation (1-year licence, OMR 300 fee, 30-day renewal notice, 400 m2 site, concrete floor, governorate approves; issuing body not confirmed); Dhofar scrap order 2013; ban on scrap collection in residential areas with OMR 500 fine; Environment Authority 2021 waste-export rules. No register or report duty found. Weak.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: No Oman regime found for pawnbrokers or purchase registers on second-hand goods. Only used-car selling permit rules (Muscat Municipality 2018; Sohar order 2019 limiting to industrial areas, OMR 100 fine). Unverified.

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Nothing new beyond K05. Precious metals and stones AML supervision regulation exists (Gazette issue 1473, text garbled, date unconfirmed); Royal Decree 30/2016 is the AML law.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: NCSI figures via Oman Daily: about 1,527 vehicle-parts establishments to end Apr 2024, of which 671 retail used parts. No licensing, register or environmental take-back rule found. Unverified.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: Only a camel digital ID / microchip plan (Oman Observer, undated) and Muscat Municipality abattoir hours. No mandatory trader register found. Unverified.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Municipal abattoirs (Muscat Municipality) serve individuals and meat shops; no private abattoir or butcher reporting duty found. Nothing actionable.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: Only 2016 ministerial decisions (194/2016 ban on exporting Omani bee breeds, fine OMR 500-1000; 209/2016 hive movement ban, expired) and a subsidised hive programme. No beekeeper register or health certificate rule found. Tiny market. Weak.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: Vet Practice Law RD 22/2017 with regulation MD 23/2021 (ministry register, licence renewal); Veterinary Preparations Law RD 34/2017 with regulation MD 60/2023 and fee decision MD 67/2023 (Gazette 1485, 19 Mar 2023). No record-keeping duty details seen; group is small. Weak/unverified.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Wells and Aflaj regulation MD 264/2000 amended by MD 193/2023: contractors must register and are classified by capacity. About 6,660 water licences to end-2024, of which 3,990 well licences, 2,280 well registrations, 151 drilling-contractor applications. Small buyer group, ministry-run process.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: APSR Decision 31/2025 licensing independent water/wastewater tanker operators (see candidate C1). Muscat Municipality sewage-vehicle health rules published 29 Jun 2026. Be'ah holds the municipal waste monopoly; governorates taking over container collection from 1 Dec (year unconfirmed). No septage manifest found.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: Occupational safety regulation (2008, amended by MoL MD 4/2021): boilers tested every 12 months, steam and air receivers every 24 months by a competent person, with a register of test date, technician and remarks (Curtis blog 2016, current force unconfirmed). No Oman lift-inspection source found. Weak.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: Water and Wastewater Sector Regulation Law RD 40/2023 (6-month transition for regulated activities, extendable 6 months). Covered through the tanker candidate C1; no separate private small-system reporting duty found.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Pesticide Law RD 64/2006; regulation MD 41/2012; MD 160/2023 replaced the lists with List A (prohibited, holders must dispose within 6 months) and List B (restricted). The ministry issued 225 retail fertiliser sale licences and 96 pesticide registration certificates in one year (year unconfirmed); North Batinah ran 6,097 inspection visits. No mandatory sales register found. Weak.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Social Development MD 405/2025 (20 Nov 2025) created an association of recruitment offices; the new domestic-worker decision bans recruitment fees and requires e-registered contracts. Office licensing rules and office count not found. See candidate C2.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: Interior Ministry cemetery regulation, Gazette 1544 (2024): municipality permits cemeteries and keeps the grave register; death report needed for burial. Municipal function, no private funeral-service licensing regime found. Not a software buyer.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Ministry of Social Development supervises 173 associations (68 Omani Women's Association branches, 42 charities, 40 professional, 23 expatriate community clubs; Oman Daily 2024). A Civil Society Institutions Law with exemptions was reported by Al Rai (date unconfirmed); annual audited accounts reviewed by the ministry under the 2001 law. Small, institutional buyers. Weak. No halal supervision body found.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: 22,242 school buses (Oman Observer, 13 Sep 2026); rented school buses need a vehicle operating card, a maximum age of 12 years, and drivers aged 23-60 with 5 years' experience. Carriage by Land regulation amended 2023: tracking systems required for goods carriers; MTCIT Naql platform for licences. Taxis stay rejected (K13). See candidates C3 and C4.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Money Services Business regulation published Apr 2024 (CBO) covers exchange houses, but they are few and licensed. Market traders and street vendors were not searched, so that part is not_reached.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Nurseries: 355 nurseries, 8,706 children (mid-2024); Social Development ministerial decision 48/2017 sets fees (OMR 100 a year individuals, OMR 200 companies); the minister was reported studying home nursery licensing (date unknown). Driving schools: Royal Oman Police 2024 regulation covers instruction offences (age 18, no night lessons 22:00-06:00). Tattoo studios, food producers and hunting outfitters not searched.

coverage.found: New fuel-station framework, Ministerial Decision 142/2025 (Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Investment Promotion), in force 6 May 2026: four categories (integrated, commercial, smart self-service, mobile), 3-year renewable licence, applications via marketing companies, fines up to OMR 3,000 and OMR 500/month for expired licences; one report mentions a one-year regularisation window for existing stations (the Times of Oman fetch did not confirm it). Owner pool is small and the duties are one-off licensing, so no recurring register found. LPG distribution not covered by results (unverified). Weak candidate C07.

coverage.category: 22. Grain, coffee, cocoa and other commodity traders, millers and warehouses
coverage.found: Nothing usable. Grain is concentrated in state-linked Oman Flour Mills and Salalah Mills. One item mentions 71 food warehouse permits in South Al Batinah in 2025 (regulator unnamed). No small-trader recurring register found.

coverage.category: 23. Co-operatives, credit unions and savings groups
coverage.found: Only consumer co-operatives (closed joint-stock form, MOCIIP licence, branches allowed). Agricultural and fishermen's co-operatives are mentioned only in an undated deck. No credit-union or savings-group law found. Few entities, so weak (C13).

coverage.category: 24. Private clinics, labs and other health providers that bill insurers or state schemes
coverage.found: MoH private health establishment licence renewal is on the e-health portal (renew from 1 month before expiry to 1 month after, then a penalty; centre OMR 450 Muscat / OMR 300 elsewhere). New fee structure announced and a 2024 decision (MD 231/2024) requires a bank guarantee. Insurer billing is Dhamani, already rejected as K10. Nothing new beyond K10 for billing. Renewal calendar only is weak (C09).

coverage.category: 25. Pharmacies, medicine importers, and users of controlled chemicals or precursors
coverage.found: Pharmacy executive regulations MD 113/2020 and fee schedule exist (pharmacy renewal OMR 300). No national track-and-trace mandate (K09). No 'precursor' list found, but Environment Authority Decision 50/2023 (hazardous chemicals) requires an environmental permit to import, sell, distribute or use, with semi-annual reports, a chemical database, SDS and Civil Defence storage/transport licences. See C05.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: Security guard services need a royal-decree licence (RD 24/99, 25/99, with ROP approval). Labour-supply licence under the Labour Law. Cleaning establishments need MD 115/2020 conditions to bring in expat workers. Current licence categories and reporting are unverified. Related duties: Omanisation (C04), permit late fines (C11). Weak (C12).

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: Tender Board Decision 104/2022 (classification and registration of contractors, suppliers, consultants); ICV principle (10% local value) in government tenders; JSRS registration for oil and gas suppliers; ICV certificate in energy was in a pilot with 2025 rollout (status unverified). Contractor classification and ICV reporting could be a niche but are not confirmed as recurring for small firms (C14, weak/unverified).

coverage.category: 28. Notaries, land agents, real estate brokers and other professionals with periodic or anti-money-laundering reports
coverage.found: Real estate brokers and developers: MoHUP Ministerial Decision 244/2022 (Gazette 1473, 25 Dec 2022), replacing 113/2021, imposes AML/CFT duties (customer due diligence, beneficial owner, written risk assessment, policies, internal audit, staff training, reporting to the National Centre for Financial Information). A draft Real Estate Regulation Law (Oman Daily, 25 July 2026) would unify brokerage, valuation, off-plan and escrow, status unknown. Lease registration at the municipality (3% fee, penalty three times the fee) and RD 12/2025 amendments are a landlord duty. See C02, C03.

coverage.category: 29. Hotels, guest houses and short-term rentals: guest registers, tourism levies
coverage.found: Strongest finding. Tourism Law Executive Regulation, Ministerial Decision 1152/2/1/141/2026, in force 17 April 2026, repeals the previous regulations; existing licensees have 6 months (about 17 October 2026). Duties: 4% tourism fee remitted quarterly with auditor-certified statements; 8% service charge distributed to staff in cash with a statement to the Ministry (circular in force 30 July 2026); annual tourism fee declaration within 3 months of year end; audited accounts within 2 months; responsible manager; electronic link with the Ministry and ROP; 3-year classification certificate for restaurants/cafes. Hotels must also send guest and visitor data daily to ROP via an online portal (older rule). Fines OMR 500-6,000. Short-term rental licensing exists via MHT. See C01.

coverage.category: 30. Small exporters and importers facing traceability or certification rules: food, fish, timber, forest-risk commodities
coverage.found: Fish exports need a Fish Quality Control Centre number, catch certificate (EU catch certificate via Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources, free, 1-3 days), and lists of boat users attached to small-boat licences. No new mandate found; import side is covered by K01. Weak (C10).

coverage.category: 31. Omanisation: one Omani per commercial registration (MoL 2025)
coverage.found: Ministry of Labour requirement from 5 May 2025 (mechanism 15 June 2025): every commercial registration older than 1 year must employ at least one Omani registered with the SPF. Firms with zero Omanis must submit an employment plan within 1 month of notice; 10+ staff comply in 3 months, smaller firms 6 months; sole proprietors managing the business are exempt for 1 year. Non-compliance means a ban on new work permits. MOCIIP Decision 411/2025 covers foreign-investor firms. Oman Observer (July 2026) reports over 245,000 firms with zero Omani employees. MD 602/2025 gives a 30% permit-fee discount for meeting Omanisation and doubles fees for non-compliance. See C04.

coverage.category: 32. Expatriate work-permit renewal and late-registration fines (MD 602/2025)
coverage.found: Employers fined OMR 10/month for late renewal or registration (individual employers OMR 15, corporate OMR 20), capped at OMR 500 per worker. Affects households and small firms. Overlaps K04 (household domestic-worker file) and K07 (rejected payroll). See C11.

coverage.category: 33. Tenancy and lease registration (RD 6/89 as amended by RD 12/2025, municipal registration)
coverage.found: Landlords must register leases with the municipality and pay 3% of annual rent; non-registration is fined at three times the fee; RD 12/2025 (dated 7 Jan 2025, in force after 6 months) created governorate rent-dispute committees (details unverified: only secondary sources seen). Pool of individual landlords is large but a municipal portal likely exists. See C03.

coverage.category: 34. Hazardous chemicals permits (Environment Authority Decision 50/2023)
coverage.found: Permits to import, export, use, sell or distribute hazardous chemicals (use permit up to 3 years, import/export up to 1 year), semi-annual reports, SDS, quantity limits, 7-working-day delivery rule, Civil Defence storage/transport licence. Buyer pool (paint, cleaning, pool and agri chemical dealers) is unverified. See C05.

coverage.category: 35. Waste licences (Environment Authority: import/transit Decision 51/2023, export 15/2021, hazardous waste transport fees MD 10/2017)
coverage.found: Import/transit licensees must keep records, file annual reports, log data in the Authority's electronic system and fit vehicle tracking devices (in force 1 May 2024). Domestic hazardous waste transport licence valid 2 years (fees RO 75-400 per MD 10/2017, may be superseded). Small buyer pool; no small-hauler register found. Weak (C06).

coverage.category: 36. Beneficial ownership register for LLCs and SAOCs (MOCIIP)
coverage.found: Companies must keep an internal register of 25%+ owners, update within 5 business days, make it available to the Ministry on 3 days' notice, and appoint an Oman-resident liaison. No annual filing. Sanctions: fines up to OMR 1,000 and suspension of the commercial registration. A 2026 amendment claim (six-month compliance) is unconfirmed. Legal basis conflicts between sources (MD 630/2022 or 424/2023). See C08.

coverage.category: 37. Non-profit associations: AML/CFT supervision (MoSD, Ministerial Decision 36/2023)
coverage.found: Associations and non-profit bodies must keep beneficiary and donor records (name, ID copy, address, date of birth), and cash donations over OMR 100 must go through approved channels. No Omani annual-report format found. Small buyer pool and low willingness to pay. See C07b (listed as C15).

coverage.category: 38. Tourism-classified restaurants, cafes, travel offices and tour guides (same regulation as 29)
coverage.found: Classified restaurants/cafes need a tourism classification certificate (3 years, renewal at least 60 days before expiry, OMR 200); travel offices must insure tourists on all organised trips and use licensed guides. Folded into C01 as an extra buyer group.

result.competitor: No operator-side software or service found for Oman (searched Arabic and English, including Nama Water Services). The core digital job (permit intake through digital channels, the central electronic register, tracking devices) is assigned by law to the licensees (Nama Water Services and the other regional licensees). Any portal or tracking vendor would therefore be bought by the utilities, not the operators. No public Nama tanker-permit portal was found, so this is not_reached and not disproven. Nama already holds contracts with tanker owners: the Shura Council discussed contract renewal and pricing with Nama in June 2024. That means the utility, not a third party, is the operators' channel.
result.duty: Confirmed and in force under APSR Decision 31/2025 (Official Gazette 1593, 27 Apr 2025, in force the next day). No one may operate an independent water or sewage tanker without a permit from the licensee for the area, i.e. the regional water/wastewater utility (Art. 2-3). The licensee must sign a unified SLA with the operator first. The licensee had to submit the SLA template to APSR within 90 days (Art. 4). Operator duties (Art. 6-7) are mostly one-off or physical: colour-code the tank (blue potable, green non-potable, yellow sewage) with an Arabic label, keep the permit in the vehicle, keep the vehicle and pump clean and maintained, load and discharge only at approved points, fix leaks, and supply data the licensee requests when it asks. The regulation places no periodic reporting or record-keeping duty on operators. The electronic register (permit, plate, supply/discharge points, volumes, complaints, inspections, cleaning) and the tracking devices are explicitly the licensee's duty (Art. 5). Existing operators had one year to comply, to about 28 Apr 2026. The text says nothing on permit validity or renewal. Fines for operating without a permit (Art. 8): OMR 50-5,000 for individuals and OMR 500-50,000 for legal entities, doubled for a repeat within 2 years, and up to OMR 50 a day (capped at OMR 10,000) for a continuing violation. Muscat Municipality guidelines (29 Jun 2026) add a sealed tank, the activity, capacity and valid licence shown on the vehicle, regular cleaning, and disposal only at authorised sites. No reports found of enforcement after the deadline.
result.market: Unverified. No register or statistic giving the number of independent tanker operators or tankers in Oman was found. Yellow sewage tankers are still common because many areas rely on septic tanks, so the market is plausibly in the low thousands of vehicles. Most operators are likely owner-drivers who are hard to sell software to.
result.reason: The duty is real and binding, with large fines. But the recurring compliance work (electronic register, tracking, inspections, SLA monitoring) is legally the utility's job, not the operator's. Operators face mainly one-off steps: get the permit, sign the SLA, paint and label the tank, keep the permit in the cab. After that they only answer the utility's data requests. The one-year transition ended around April 2026, so the deadline-driven rush is over. Permit renewal frequency is unknown. Buyers are owner-drivers with low willingness to pay, and the utilities are the natural channel. No competitor was found, but the opening is thin. At most a done-for-you permit-application service, or a sale to the utilities, which is out of scope.

result.competitor: The free MHT e-service 'Payment of Fee/Taxes' (sign-in via Commercial Register commissioner) already takes the quarterly 4% payment online and covers the annual declaration. Guest data goes daily to ROP through the Ministry's 'Mueen' system, and the Ministry says certified hotel management software can submit the logs automatically, so certified PMS vendors already exist for that part (names not found). The quarterly statement and annual declaration must be certified by an external auditor, so auditors are a gatekeeper and would compete as a done-for-you service. Searches in Arabic and English found no Oman-specific product that compiles the 4% statement or the 8% distribution statement. Regional accounting/PMS tools (e.g. Qoyod hotel accounting, a generic PMS) do not appear to cover the MHT format. The gap is small: computing 4%/8% is trivial in any PMS or spreadsheet.
result.duty: Confirmed in the regulation text on qanoon.om: Ministerial Decision under Tourism Law RD 69/2023, which repeals MD 124/2021. Art. 29(1): 4% tourism fee on total customer price. Art. 30: remitted quarterly with a monthly revenue and fee statement certified by the external auditor; the Q4 statement also shows the year total. Art. 29(2): 8% service charge paid in cash to staff, with a distribution statement to the Ministry. Art. 23(5): annual fee declaration within 3 months of year end, certified by the auditor. Art. 23(6): audited accounts within 2 months. Art. 23(4): electronic link with MHT/ROP. Penalties (Annex 5): late fee 10%/month capped at 100% of the fee; OMR 1,000-3,000 for service-charge breaches; OMR 2,000-5,000 for Art. 30/23(5)-(6) breaches; OMR 500-1,000 for no e-link. Art. 75(2): licence cancelled after 5 consecutive months of unpaid fees. Art. 27: restaurant/cafe classification valid 3 years, renew 60 days before expiry; hotel classification renewal period not stated. Guest houses, green/heritage inns and rest houses are covered (1-year licence, OMR 50). Holiday homes are not mentioned. Existing licensees had 6 months to comply (Oman Observer: October 2026 deadline).
result.market: NCSI (via Oman Observer) counts 1,475 hotels, hotel apartments, furnished apartments and other accommodation facilities in 2025. An older national breakdown lists about 160 guest houses, 120 green lodges (153 by end 2024), 15 heritage inns, 39 rest houses and 164 hotel apartments. Guest houses are growing fast regionally: South Al Batinah had 275 guest houses and 70 green lodges in H1 2026; Buraimi had 47 establishments. Classified restaurants/cafes add an unknown number. Total addressable: roughly 1,500-2,500 establishments, mostly micro guest houses with low ability to pay.
result.reason: The duty is real, recent and enforced: quarterly auditor-certified 4% statements, an 8% service-charge distribution statement, annual declaration, fines up to OMR 5,000 and licence cancellation. But the Ministry's own free e-service handles payment, certified PMS vendors handle the Mueen/ROP link, and the mandatory external auditor sits in the workflow and will likely sell the done-for-you service. The calculations are trivial, so differentiation is thin. The market is small (about 1,500 accommodation establishments nationally, many of them micro guest houses paying OMR 50 licences) with low willingness to pay. The 6-month transition deadline (about October 2026) gives a short-term trigger. A possible angle is a niche add-on for small guest houses (statement generator plus 8% payout log), sold through auditors and PRO bureaus.

result.competitor: I found no Oman-specific AML compliance kit for real estate brokers. Generic KYC/AML vendors that say they cover Oman do the core screening and KYC work: Shufti Pro, Focal (getfocal.ai), Arctic Intelligence (risk-assessment software), NameScan and AiPrise. One vendor says its product files STRs/CTRs to the NCFI through goAML; that is a vendor claim. I could not confirm whether Omani brokers have to report through goAML. UAE goAML-for-brokers consultancies (amluae, simplysolved) could expand into Oman.
result.duty: Real, but mostly continuous rather than calendar-driven. I read the MD 244/2022 text on qanoon.om. It repeals 113/2021 (Art. 3) and applies to brokerage offices and developers. It requires: a written risk assessment that is kept up to date and shown to the Ministry on request; customer due diligence, including beneficial owners at the 25% threshold; risk-based periodic review of customer files; written policies approved by management; a compliance officer whose details go to both the Ministry and the NCFI; ongoing staff training with no fixed frequency; suspicious transaction reports to the NCFI within 48 hours; and 10-year record keeping. The Decision sets no fines itself. Penalties come through Art. 52 of the AML/CFT Law (RD 30/2016), applied by the Ministry's Real Estate Monitoring and AML Department. The claim calls the Real Estate Regulation Law a draft. That is wrong: it was issued as RD 79/2025 and, according to a law-firm summary, has been in force since 10 Mar 2026. It replaced the 1986 brokerage law (RD 78/86), which is one of the legal bases of MD 244/2022. I could not confirm whether 244/2022 is still in force under the new law or whether new executive regulations replace it. The OMR 3,000 / 6-month penalty is for unlicensed brokering, not for AML failures. I found no evidence of how often the AML rules are enforced.
result.market: Small, and I found no official count of licensed brokerage offices. Oman Daily (25 Jul 2026) says more than 190 real estate companies were registered with MoHUP by the end of June 2026. An older, undated report mentions more than 500 unregistered firms. The likely total is a few hundred licensed brokers and developers. Not reached: the MoHUP register.
result.reason: The AML duties are real and detailed (risk assessment, CDD/beneficial owner, compliance officer, STRs within 48 hours, 10-year records). They are continuous rather than deadline-driven, and I found no evidence of enforcement or fines. The market is small: about 190 registered real estate companies plus an uncounted number of brokers, probably a few hundred buyers paying low prices. Generic KYC/AML tools that cover Oman (Shufti Pro, Focal, Arctic Intelligence) already handle screening. The legal basis is shifting: RD 79/2025 has been in force since March 2026, and new executive regulations may replace MD 244/2022, so building now is risky. A templates-plus-CDD-workflow MVP is simple, but willingness to pay and distribution are weak. It could be a bolt-on to K05 rather than a standalone product.

result.competitor: No dedicated Omanisation tracker or planner found. Search results showed only general ERP, accounting and VAT tools (TallyPrime through Ooredoo Maktabi, HisabPlus, Odoo add-ons, Wafeq). The Ministry notifies firms through its own electronic system, and the Tawteen platform links job seekers with employers. Unverified: whether the Ministry's e-services show each firm its compliance status. PRO and typing bureaus are the de facto service layer.
result.duty: One Omani per commercial registration older than 1 year, announced by the Ministry of Labour on 5 May 2025, with the enforcement mechanism set out on 15 June 2025. Deadlines: foreign-invested firms file a plan within 3 months plus at most 3 months' grace. Firms with more than 10 workers file a plan within 3 months. Firms with fewer than 10 workers have 6 months plus a case review, and can get a temporary exemption if they show local value added. Sole entrepreneurs and full-time owners get a 1-year grace period. Penalties: an automatic ban on new work permits for foreign-invested firms and firms with more than 10 workers, and an automatic ban on new licences for firms with fewer than 10 workers. MD 602/2025 cuts permit fees by 30% for firms that meet Omanisation targets and doubles them for firms that don't (reported as roughly OMR 211 rising to OMR 421; this figure comes from a March 2026 opinion piece). MOCIIP Decision 411/2025 requires foreign-owned companies to have an Omani registered with the SPF. Not reached: the official text of the decisions and any 2026 change to enforcement.
result.market: About 245,000 establishments employed zero Omanis in May 2025 (Ministry of Labour figure, via Oman Observer and Oman Daily). 152,860 small and medium enterprises were registered with the SME Development Authority (Riyada) at end-June 2025; at end-2024 that register held about 125,600 micro firms out of 145,750.
result.reason: The duty is real. On 5 May 2025 Oman's Ministry of Labour announced that every commercial registration older than one year must employ at least one Omani, and it set out the enforcement mechanism on 15 June 2025. MD 602/2025 links work-permit fees to Omanisation. I found no dedicated Omanisation planner, only general ERP, VAT and payroll tools. But the core job is hiring one Omani and registering them with the Social Protection Fund (SPF), which is a hiring and cost problem, not a paperwork problem. The Ministry sends notices through its own electronic system and applies permit bans automatically. A plan for one hire per registration is trivial, and PRO bureaus already handle the filing. Small firms are pushing back on the rule's cost and won't pay for a planner. Pain is high but software adds little.

result.reason: The decision is real: Oman Observer reports MD 574/2025. It requires written Arabic contracts registered electronically with the ministry, bans recruitment fees charged to workers, and allows three months to regularise. The article puts these duties on employers (households), not recruitment offices, and gives no penalties or effective date. MD 405/2025 created an association of recruitment offices. Gulf News does not say membership is mandatory and describes no filing duty for offices. I found no count of licensed offices (Infobel's 726 staffing records is not specific). I found no competitor software. The ministry's own platform, and the Chamber's "Istiqdam" platform work, probably cover contract registration. The buyer pool is small and the office-level recurring duty is unproven, so I am keeping the score at 3.

Duty is real: the MoE rented-bus rules (2020, amended by decision 190/2021) require a valid registration, an MTCIT operating card, insurance, a bus no more than 12 years old, and an Omani driver aged 23-60 with 5 years' experience. Tracking is required on request. Newer tenders ask for 2023 or later buses with tracking, cameras and sensors. A Sept 2026 report counts 22,242 buses. Contracts are renewed after inspection committees check them. I found no dedicated compliance software. Weak points: the buyers are mostly owner-drivers with few vehicles, little willingness to pay, a government-driven tracking/hardware mandate, and the ministry is building its own digital tools. Renewal happens yearly through the schools and directorates, so reminders add little.

The duty is real. The landlord must register the lease with the municipality within one month, at a 3% fee, with a fine of 3x the fee, and the contract is void before government bodies if unregistered. Muscat Municipality already offers online registration, renewal, amendment and cancellation through Oman Business and its own app and website. Sanad offices and real estate offices also handle it. In Dec 2025 the Interior Ministry set up an electronic system for rental disputes, so the state already covers both halves of the idea. Landlords file one lease at a time, so there is little recurring workflow to sell. A tracker would be a thin add-on and landlords are unlikely to pay for it. Not verified: the fee rate (an older 5% decision exists), market size, and the text of RD 12/2025.

Duty is real and in force. Decision 50/2023 took effect 1 May 2023. It requires environmental permits to import, export, use, make, sell or distribute hazardous chemicals. Import/export permits last up to 1 year and use permits up to 3 years. Permit holders must file a semi-annual report electronically in the Authority's form (Art. 14). The report fine is only OMR 200 (Annex 2), and unpermitted import/use is OMR 1,000. Weak points: the penalty is low, there are two filings a year, and the report goes through an Environment Authority e-system I could not identify. The state system probably covers the core job. No third-party competitor was searched. Market size was not found, and the buyer group is likely small and mixed. Treat as a niche, low-urgency compliance reminder or consulting add-on.

result.reason: The duty is real. MD 424/2023 replaced MD 630/2022 and has been in force since 7 Aug 2023. It requires a UBO register at the 25% threshold, with fines up to OMR 1,000 and CR suspension of up to 3 months. But the claim's premise, an internal-only register with no filing, looks outdated. The Mercator and CMS summaries describe a mandatory online UBO registration on MOCIIP's Oman Business Platform. That free state portal covers the core job, including KYC for non-resident UBOs. The duty is one-off plus updates on change, so frequency is low. I found no commercial UBO software, but the state portal plus a spreadsheet leaves little to sell. The "2026 amendment" appears only in Global Law Experts and is unverified. I did not check the platform's own pages.

Duty is real: the MoH page lets a private health establishment renew from 1 month before to 1 month after expiry. Later renewal brings a fine (30 OMR clinics, 70 OMR centres/polyclinics, 200 OMR hospitals). Renewal is done through the MoH eHealth portal, which processes it immediately. The portal already does the filing, so only a reminder layer is left, and that is thin. Renewal is annual-ish, with low penalties and few documents. About 1,700 private establishments (2022, excluding pharmacies), so the market is small. MD 231/2024 is the executive regulation of the medical-profession law, not a fee or bank-guarantee decision, so the claim's trigger is partly mislabelled. Fees come from a separate decision. Overlaps rejected K10. Low score.
